title: Energetic Cost of Temporal Information Processing in Quantum Reservoirs
authors: Gabriele Cenedese, Gonzalo Manzano, Gian Luca Giorgi, Roberta Zambrini
abstract: Quantum reservoir computing offers a promising route toward energy-efficient machine learning by processing temporal information with minimal training overhead. Yet, the physical principles linking its energetic cost to computational performance remain largely unexplored. Here we show that, in an interacting spin reservoir, information encoding and information processing are governed by distinct physical mechanisms. In the weak interacting regime, we derive an analytical expression for the average (switching) work, showing that the energetic cost of encoding new inputs is determined by the local response of the reservoir units. In contrast, interactions primarily redistribute the encoded information, generating memory and nonlinear features while only weakly affecting the work. This separation produces opposite correlations between energetic cost and performance for representative linear and nonlinear benchmark tasks. Our results identify the switching work as the energetic signature of information encoding and clarify when energetic efficiency and computational performance are compatible.
summary: This paper analyzes the energetic cost of temporal data processing in Quantum Reservoir Computing using an interacting spin reservoir model. It shows that information encoding is characterized by a measurable switching work ($	ext{W}_k$), which can be analytically derived under weak coupling assumptions. The findings reveal a crucial separation between energy expenditure and computational capability, offering guidelines for designing energy-efficient quantum machine learning systems.
main_problem: The study aims to understand the physical principles governing the energetic cost associated with temporal information processing in Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC). Specifically, it seeks to clarify when energy efficiency aligns with computational performance.
main_result: The work done during input encoding is identified as the switching work ($	ext{W}_k$), which is governed by local reservoir unit responses. This leads to an anti-correlation between energetic cost and performance for different types of tasks (linear vs. nonlinear).
method: The authors derive analytical expressions for the average switching work using weak-interaction approximations within the framework of the GKLS master equation.
model_or_system: The system is an interacting spin reservoir composed of $N$ spin-1/2 particles, governed by a Hamiltonian including local fields and pairwise interactions. Dynamics are described by the GKLS master equation, analyzed in the weak interacting regime.
key_observables: Switching Work ($	ext{W}_k$), Heat ($	ext{Q}_k$), Computational Capacity ($C$), and thermodynamic quantities like entropy production ($\Sigma_k$).
important_parameters: Interaction strength ($J_{ij}$), local field amplitude ($a_k$), disorder strength ($D$), and the ratio $J_s/h$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the weak interacting regime approximation, assuming a piecewise-constant driving protocol for work calculation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how switching work ($\langle W_k angle$) and computational capacity vary with input amplitude ($h$) and interaction strength ($J_s/h$) for different tasks (STM, PC).
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first establishing the Hamiltonian and dynamics, then deriving analytical expressions for $	ext{W}_k$ in the weak coupling limit. It subsequently applies these results to benchmark tasks, demonstrating the separation of encoding work from information processing mechanisms.
why_interesting: This work directly connects fundamental concepts from open quantum systems (work extraction, dissipation) to modern machine learning paradigms (reservoir computing), providing physical constraints on energy-efficient computation.
